animal in several respects, most notably in enlargement of eyes,
reduction of the gut, addition of natatory chaetae, and reor-
ganization of the musculature, with the most drastic changes
occurring in Autolytinae. The stolons die after breeding. Differ-
ent stolon types are characterized based on their head shape and
appendages: illustrations and a summary on different stolons
can be found in San Martin (2014). Schizogamy, in turn, may
be divided in two types; scissiparity where stolons are devel-
oped from already existing segments, and gemmiparity where
the stolon formation is achieved by newly added segments. Both
types occur within Autolytinae and Syllinae. Reproduction takes
place in the free water, either by broadcast spawning, or as in
the nuptial dance of some Autolytinae where the male stolon
swims around and entangles the female stolon with sperm in
mucus threads (Gidholm, 1965). A striking pattern of stoloniza-
tion occurs in Syllis ramosa and in Ramisyllis multicaudata; both
animals live in sponges where many stolons are formed in a
complex branching pattern and penetrate the canal system of
their host sponge (Glasby et al., 2012; Okada, 1937; Schroed-
er et al., 2017). The internal anatomy of Ramisyllis multicaudata
and the implications of the external bifurcated branching on the
myoanatomy and the neuroanatomy were recently described in.
detail by Ponz-Segrelles et al. (2021). Ponz-Segrelles et al. (2018;
2020) have also studied the gene expression during the different
reproductive stages of syllids and have found similar gene expres-
sion profiles for female and non-reproducing individuals, while
male gene expression was different.

There is evidence for direct sperm transfer with sper-
matophores and even internal fertilization with male copulatory
chaetae in several small, interstitial Syllidae (Franke, 1999; Kuper
and Westheide, 1997a; b). Brooding is also common and vari-
able. Epigamic Syllidae have direct development where the eggs
and sometimes the larvae may remain attached to the female (in
Exogoninae and Eusyllinae) (Figs. 11.1b, d). In schizogamic Syl-
lidae, such as Autolytus, the female stolons brood the larvae in
ventral egg sacs for some time before dying. An extreme mode is
displayed by Syllis vivipara that broods the young in the coelom
in the posterior part of the body. In due course, the juveniles
emerge by breaking off from the posterior end. The endocrine
control of Syllidae reproduction appears to involve prostomi-
al stolon—or epigamy-promoting hormones and proventricular
hormones that inhibit the sexual development (see Franke and
Pfannenstiel (1984) and references within). All known Syllidae
have non-feeding larvae and records of planktotrophy until now
appear to be erroneous (Rouse, 2000c).
